activities.description: Johan Rockström stands on a stage giving a presentation.
He gestures with his hands while speaking.
He reads a quote from his phone.

characterInteraction.description: Johan addresses the audience directly, engaging them with passion and expressive gestures.

scenes.contextualRelevance: Explains the significant role of the present generation in acknowledging and acting upon environmental changes.

mood.description: Excited at the beginning; transitions to Pensive and ends with a touch of Anxious.

keyMoments.changeDescription: Shift from Excited to Pensive as Johan acknowledges past doubts.
Shift to Anxious as the quote highlights rapid change and nervousness.

narrativeProgression.description: Johan Rockström introduces the concept of the Anthropocene and the urgency for action.
He claims humanity is at the 'end of the curve' and has 'hit the ceiling' in terms of environmental impact.
He emphasizes growing awareness of the Anthropocene.
Mentions the Economist's recognition of the Anthropocene and highlights a quote from the publication.

trimmingSuggestions.description: Shorten the ending sequence with logos and website address.

text_to_speech: - Today, dear friends, we are the first generation to stand on the top of a mountain of evidence of exponential rise of pressures. We're the first generation with absolutely no excuse to act, but in 1962 you could almost excuse those who said, look here, we don't really believe that it has to go this wrong because Rachel Carson was just at the beginning of the curve. We are not in the beginning of the curve, we're at the end of the curve. We've hit the ceiling. So, dear friends, welcome to the Anthropocene. Now the good news is that this starting to be understood. Around the world you see ample, ample media, policy, business recognizing that we are in this new geological epoch. It started actually with The Economist, as you see the front page here, welcoming humanity to the Anthropocene. The Economist as you may know is this beautiful, eloquent, strict British weekly, so influential in the economic business world. I'm great admirer of The Economist. It has these kind of British understatement type language which I find so convincing sometimes, and there's a quote in here which reflected so well and still reflects how we scientists feel today, and it says as follows, "When things are changing faster "than science stipulates it should, "a certain degree of nervousness is a reasonable response." (laughing) British understatement, and that's exactly what we're seeing. Things are changing faster than science stipulates it should. Not a certain, but a significant degree of nervousness is a reasonable response. So, dear friends, welcome to the Anthropocene.

youtube_description:
Earth's new epoch. Watch the full talk: https://ehf.nz/johan18b

Johan Rockström is the founding director of the Stockholm Resilience Centre (http://www.stockholmresilience.org) and incoming director of Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (https://www.pik-potsdam.de/). 

Filmed at New Frontiers (https://www.newfrontiers.nz) in New Zealand, hosted by the Edmund Hillary Fellowship (https://www.ehf.org).
